argument:
Philosophy in the Latin West of the eleventh and twelfth centuries was done by people who already believed. Monotheism ran the institutions, so the great minds of the period spent their energy adjusting Plato or Aristotle until the fit was comfortable: Plotinus and Augustine before them, Philo of Alexandria squaring Plato with the Torah. After Rome fell into a Greek Byzantine East and a Latin West, Europe developed scholasticism, less a doctrine than a method, built on dialectic, the conversational back and forth Socrates used. Stephen West opens by insisting that "God" is not one fixed idea. Plato meant something different from a modern Christian. The Stoics meant the universe, Plotinus the transcendent One. He describes his own year reading every proof he could find, at 17 and homeless, genuinely open to either answer.

Anselm of Canterbury, called the father of scholasticism, thought in terms of two kinds of existence: things in human understanding alone, and things in reality. An invention still on the drawing board sits in the first category. A lawnmower or a Honda Civic with the muffler removed sits in both. A beetle nobody has found yet, deep in the Amazon, sits in reality without sitting in anyone's mind at all.

From that division comes the most famous proof of God's existence ever written. Anselm sets a trap, and the host walks the listener into it. Grant, hypothetically, that God is that than which nothing greater can be thought. Almost everyone grants it, atheists most eagerly, since it sounds like a description of a fantasy. But if you understand the phrase, the thing exists in your thought. And a thing existing in reality is greater than the same thing existing in thought alone. So the greatest conceivable thing cannot exist in thought alone, or it would not be the greatest conceivable thing. Therefore it exists.

Most people sense something wrong and cannot name it. Immanuel Kant named it, centuries later, and gave the argument its label. Why should existing count as greater, other than as a human bias in favor of existing? And existence is not a property the way yellow is. A banana is yellow, thin and calorie dense; adding "and it exists" smuggles in the conclusion, like defining a fruit called a washington as green, round, peelable and real. Gaunilo, a monk and a believer, had already made the point with a perfect island. Anselm's defenders answer that there is no perfect number of trees, though there may be perfect goodness.

Moses Maimonides, writing in the 1100s, pushed the other way. The Torah calls God he, father, speaker, because Moses had to reach people who had never heard of one God at all. Maimonides denies God has attributes of any kind, since parts invite the question of what joined them. We can say only what God is not. Helping ducks across a road makes the host benevolent; calling God benevolent in that same word is an insult to both.
keyIdeas: Atheists who dismiss God by mocking a childhood, popular conception of God are only refuting one narrow definition, ignoring the many other philosophical concepts of God that thinkers have developed.

Anselm distinguishes things that exist only in human understanding from things that exist in reality, then argues that a being 'than which nothing greater can be thought' must exist in reality too, since existing in reality is greater than existing in thought alone.

Kant objected that treating existence-in-reality as automatically greater than existence-in-thought is just a human bias, and that existence is not a quality like other attributes -- his invented 'washington' fruit shows that defining something as existing doesn't make it exist.

Gaunilo's 'perfect island' used Anselm's same reasoning to 'prove' the existence of a perfect island, suggesting something is wrong with the argument's form; the counter-response is that qualities like the amount of sand or number of trees don't admit of a true maximum the way goodness and justice do.

Maimonides argued Moses used human, physical language for God because his audience wasn't ready for an abstract God, and that God cannot have any qualities at all -- since qualities imply parts, and parts raise the question of what brought them together -- so it is more accurate to describe God only negatively, e.g. 'not merciless' rather than 'benevolent.'

terms.def: Anselm's proof that God, defined as the greatest conceivable being, must exist in reality and not merely in thought.
The medieval method of acquiring knowledge through dialectical reasoning, of which Anselm is considered the father.
Kant's invented fruit whose definition includes 'and it exists,' used to show that defining existence into a thing doesn't make it real.
A parody of Anselm's argument applying the same logic to 'prove' a perfect island exists, meant to expose a flaw in its form.
Maimonides' view that God can only be described by what he is not, since positive qualities wrongly categorize God's absolute oneness.

anchors: they were proving God didn’t exist, or at least making fun of the idea of a God existing, based on a very limited view of what God is
Let’s say you have an idea for an invention, and it exists only in your mind because you haven’t actually created it yet
if it exists only in thought it could also be thought of as existing in reality as well, which is greater
That sounds a lot like a bias inherent in a human that values existing over not existing
This sort of tacking existence on after the fact is what Kant said Anselm did in his ontological argument
you can use the exact same argument to prove that lots of other things exist that don’t actually exist
there can be a perfect goodness and justice, and these are the qualities Anselm was proving the existence of with his argument
the people of his time period weren’t familiar with the idea of a monotheistic, personal God
If multiple parts exist in any sense, the question “What brought those two parts together?” becomes valid
To put God’s benevolence on the same level as mine for helping some ducks across the road is completely ridiculous to Maimonides
how ridiculous would it be to think that when Plato talked about God he had the same concept in his mind as a modern-day Christian or Jew
he could equally be proving the existence of Plotinus’ transcendent One or Good, which didn’t have any human characteristics

whenever one of these guys asserts something to be absolutely true—like, they preface what they’re saying with “obviously” or “certainly”—most of the time that’s the portion of the argument that I take issue with the most
all the same fallacies are present in that argument. They’re just in different places
Just how you can’t be born into modern times and allow modern social conventions to tell you what justice is
like Averroes pointed out last episode, can we expect the average person to go through that kind of schooling and to understand the underlying concepts of religion in depth
I want you guys to have a conversation with Saint Anselm and let him convince you that God existed
there are obvious similarities between this conception of God and Plotinus’ transcendent One. This is the same thing Lao Tzu and Chuang Tzu said about the Tao
That is the object of language, to convey a specific idea
I prefer to extricate that intelligent man from his embarrassment and show him the cause of his perplexity, so that he may attain perfection and be at peace
